item.title: The 500ms Delay That Exposed the XZ Backdoor
item.description:
You can hide the code, but you still have to execute it.

Summary

In March 2024, the XZ Utils backdoor was discovered after Andres Freund noticed something that looked like a performance problem rather than a security incident.

While investigating PostgreSQL performance on Debian Sid, Freund noticed that SSH logins were taking roughly 500 milliseconds longer than expected and that sshd was consuming unusual CPU time.

That small anomaly led him to investigate further.

item.title: The Archive That Exposed the Operator
item.description:
The attacker didn’t get caught because Tor failed. He got caught because he uploaded too much.

Summary

In 2020, the Vastaamo psychotherapy center in Finland suffered a major data breach affecting tens of thousands of patients.

The attacker, operating under the name Ransom Man, attempted to extort Vastaamo and later began publishing stolen patient records.

One of the major OPSEC failures occurred when the attacker attempted to make the stolen data easier to distribute.

item.title: The Backup File That Exposed the ClickFix Operation
item.description:
A forgotten backup file exposed the source code and internal infrastructure of a ClickFix operation.

Summary

The ClickFix campaign was using its own web infrastructure to distribute malware and track infections.

From the outside, the infrastructure looked like another suspicious ClickFix domain.

Then a simple enumeration revealed something that should never have been publicly accessible: An old PHP backup file.

The file was:

/api/index.php.bak

It contained part of the application’s source code.

item.title: The Bug Bounty Account That Exposed the Persona
item.description:
The alias was supposed to hide the person. The same alias helped investigators find him.

Summary

TeamPCP operated through several online aliases, including DeadCatx3.

One of those aliases wasn’t only used in the group’s criminal activity.

It also appeared on HackerOne, a legitimate bug bounty platform.

That gave investigators something valuable: a place where the same username existed outside the criminal ecosystem.

From there, the investigation moved from an alias to a real name, then to other accounts and eventually to a real-world persona. Flare assessed with high confidence that the operator behind DeadCatx3 was Ruben Thomson and said the findings were confirmed with law enforcement.

item.title: The Default Cobalt Strike Setup That Exposed the Team Server
item.description:
The operator thought about hiding the Beacon. The defender looked at the server.

Summary

Cobalt Strike is designed to provide operators with a flexible command-and-control infrastructure.

Its Malleable C2 functionality allows Beacon traffic to be customized so that malicious communications can resemble normal web traffic.

But customization is only useful if the operator actually changes the defaults.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 demonstrated that Cobalt Strike Team Servers using default or recognizable configurations could be identified remotely through active network probing.

item.title: The Email Address That Led Back to the Administrator
item.description:
The administrator had a pseudonym. His email history didn’t.

Summary

Conor Brian Fitzpatrick was the administrator of BreachForums, operating online under the name pompompurin.

He used VPNs and different online identities to separate himself from the forum.

But investigators eventually found connections between those identities and Fitzpatrick’s real-world identity.

One of the important starting points was an email address.

The OPSEC Failure

While communicating with the administrator of RaidForums, the person behind pompompurin mentioned his real name and an email address:

item.title: The Metadata Threat Actor Forgot to Remove
item.description:
You removed what people could see. You forgot what the file could reveal.

Summary

Metadata is information stored inside or alongside a file that may not be visible when the file is opened normally.

A document can contain an author’s name. An image can contain GPS coordinates. A file can contain timestamps, software information, usernames, device information, revision history, or other details about how it was created.

The information may not appear in the content itself, but anyone who obtains the original file may be able to extract it.

item.title: The Open Directory That Exposed the Operator's Toolbox
item.description:
The server was supposed to deliver files. Instead, it delivered the operation.

Summary

A threat actor exposed an internet-facing server with directory listing enabled, this happen when the threat actor want to infiltrate tools/data/etc, but lazy to setup a secure environment so they just use pyhton http.server

The OPSEC Failure

The server looked like a normal file server. It was running a Python HTTP server on port 8000, 8080, 8081, 8181 or other common http-alt ports, as default Python http.server will enable the directory listing, if not use correctly the /home/user/ exposed leaving .bash_history, .config, and other sensitive files

item.title: The Phishing CDN That Became a Backdoor
item.description:
OPSEC Failure: The phishing infrastructure exposed a CDN component that could mirror files and write PHP, leaving the operator’s own server vulnerable to takeover.

Summary

The investigation started with a phishing-as-a-service operation.

The service allowed customers to create phishing pages and use them to collect credentials from victims. The infrastructure included a separate CDN/API component hosted at api.gifan.id.

At first, the CDN looked like supporting infrastructure.

Then its functionality became interesting.

item.title: The Scam APK That Led Back to Its Developer
item.description:
The malware infrastructure was connected to the operator through reused identity and infrastructure clues.

Summary

The investigation started with an Android application called “LIHAT Foto Paket”, distributed through a package-delivery scam.

The application looked like a simple package-tracking application, but It wasn’t.

Analysis showed that the APK requested SMS permissions and communicated with infrastructure controlled through randiramli.com. When an SMS arrived on the infected device, the application sent the message contents back to the remote server.

item.title: The Threat Actor Who Infected Himself
item.description:
He spent his time stealing information from victims. Then an info-stealer stole his.

Summary

Threat actors often rely on information stealers to collect credentials, cookies, browser data, and other information from victims.

In this case, the same type of malware ended up on the threat actor’s own computer.

Hudson Rock reported that a prominent threat actor accidentally infected his own machine with an information stealer.

Instead of becoming another anonymous victim, the infection exposed information connected to the actor and his operations.
